opening: Lord, meet us gently today and always
body:
In Ezekiel 37, God says His people will never again be two nations, but one, with one king over them. He is referring to the old division of the United Kingdom (Israel) under Solomon.  It was divided between Judah and the northern kingdom, often represented by Ephraim/Joseph.  Ezekiel was prophesying that the two kingdoms would be united again by God.  His point was reunification, not just survival.
Next, Ezekiel 18 adds the moral side of restoration: “Cast away from you all the crimes you have committed, and make for yourselves a new heart and a new spirit.” So reunion is not just political or national. The people also have to turn from sin. God is not only promising to gather them; He is calling them to repentance and interior change.

Then in John 11, after Lazarus is raised, Caiaphas says it is better that one man die instead of the people. He means it politically, as a way to protect the nation. But John says Caiaphas was actually prophesying without realizing it: Jesus would die for the nation, and not only for the nation, but also to gather into one the dispersed children of God. That language of “gather into one” sounds very much like Ezekiel’s promise that the divided people will no longer remain split.
Something really interesting follows in Ezekiel 37:15-28 the two sticks Ezekiel makes that image concrete. God tells Ezekiel to take one stick for Judah and one for Joseph/Ephraim, then join them so they become one stick in his hand. God explains that this means He will gather His scattered people and make them one nation again. So the two sticks are really a visual sign of the healing of division.  Now just a little stretch, when Caiaphas declares that one man die, Jesus no longer walks in public among the Jews.  In fact, he left for the region near the desert, to a town called Ephraim.  A slight connection to the name of the two sticks (one labeled Judah, the other Joseph/Ephraim–the latter was the dominant tribe of the remaining ten tribes of the northern Kingdom at the time).
So the connection is this:
Ezekiel speaks of a divided people being made one and of the need for a new heart and spirit. John shows that this unity will come through the death of Christ. Caiaphas thinks he is talking about preserving one nation politically, but John shows that Jesus will actually die to gather God’s scattered people into one.
So for us today, we are still waiting to be fully reunited with God, and while we wait we are called to repent, cast away our sins, and turn back to Him. That waiting is not passive. It means making new the heart and spirit, so that we are no longer living divided from Him.
